steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the lead section of an encyclopedia article on the abacus: what it is, how it represents numbers and is used for calculation, and where it is still used today.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Definition and history of use
- Physical construction
- How numbers are represented
- Calculation methods
- Decline and present-day use

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Definition
  - abacus (abaci or abacuses), aka counting frame; hand-operated calculating tool
  - used from ancient times: ancient Near East, Europe, China, Russia
  - largely replaced by handheld electronic calculators in the 1980s; some attempts to revive use
- Construction
  - two-dimensional array of slidable beads (or similar objects)
  - earliest: loose on flat surface or sliding in grooves
  - later: beads slide on rods, built into a frame -> faster manipulation
- Representing numbers
  - each rod = one digit of multi-digit number; positional numeral system, e.g. base ten (some cultures other bases)
  - Roman and East Asian abacuses: like bi-quinary coded decimal; top deck (1 or 2 beads) = fives, bottom deck (4 or 5 beads) = ones
  - natural numbers normally; some allow simple fractions (Roman abacus); imagined decimal point -> fixed-point arithmetic
- Calculation
  - addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, square and cube roots; multiple methods per design
  - arrange beads for a number, manipulate with another number, read result (or use as start for next operation)
- Decline / use today
  - practical tool in ancient world; widely used in Europe until 17th century
  - fell out of use with decimal notation and algorismic methods
  - calculators/computers now common, but still everyday use in some countries
  - no writing implement/paper (needed for algorism) or power source needed
  - merchants, traders, clerks in parts of Eastern Europe, Russia, China, Africa
  - scoring system in non-electronic table games
  - visual impairment preventing calculator use
  - teaching math fundamentals to children: Japan, China

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
An abacus (abaci or abacuses), which is also called a counting frame, is a calculating tool that is operated by hand. It was used from ancient times in the ancient Near East, Europe, China, and Russia, until handheld electronic calculators mostly replaced it during the 1980s, and there have been some attempts to bring back its use. An abacus is made of a two-dimensional array of beads (or similar objects) that can slide. In the earliest designs the beads could be loose on a flat surface or slide in grooves. Later the beads were made to slide on rods and were built into a frame, which made it faster to move them.

Usually each rod stands for one digit of a number with multiple digits, laid out with a positional numeral system like base ten (but some cultures used other numerical bases). Roman and East Asian abacuses use a system that is like bi-quinary coded decimal, where a top deck (with one or two beads) represents fives and a bottom deck (with four or five beads) represents ones. Normally natural numbers are used, but some abacuses allow simple fractional parts (for example in the Roman abacus), and you can imagine a decimal point to do fixed-point arithmetic.

- Calculation
  - addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, square and cube roots; multiple methods per design
  - arrange beads for a number, manipulate with another number, read result (or start of next operation)
- Decline / use today
  - practical tool in ancient world; Europe until 17th century
  - fell out of use with decimal notation and algorismic methods
  - still everyday use in some countries despite calculators/computers
  - no writing implement/paper (algorism) or power source needed
  - merchants, traders, clerks in parts of Eastern Europe, Russia, China, Africa
  - scoring in non-electronic table games; visual impairment
  - teaching children: Japan, China

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
An abacus (abaci or abacuses), which is also called a counting frame, is a calculating tool that is operated by hand. It was used from ancient times in the ancient Near East, Europe, China, and Russia, until handheld electronic calculators mostly replaced it during the 1980s, and there have been some attempts to bring back its use. An abacus is made of a two-dimensional array of beads (or similar objects) that can slide. In the earliest designs the beads could be loose on a flat surface or slide in grooves. Later the beads were made to slide on rods and were built into a frame, which made it faster to move them.

Usually each rod stands for one digit of a number with multiple digits, laid out with a positional numeral system like base ten (but some cultures used other numerical bases). Roman and East Asian abacuses use a system that is like bi-quinary coded decimal, where a top deck (with one or two beads) represents fives and a bottom deck (with four or five beads) represents ones. Normally natural numbers are used, but some abacuses allow simple fractional parts (for example in the Roman abacus), and you can imagine a decimal point to do fixed-point arithmetic.

There are multiple methods to do calculations with any particular abacus design, including addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and square and cube roots. First the beads are arranged to represent a number, then they are moved to do a mathematical operation with another number, and the final position of the beads can be read as the result (or it can be used as the starting number for the next operations).

Abacuses were a practical calculating tool in the ancient world. The abacus was used widely in Europe until as late as the 17th century, but it fell out of use when decimal notation and algorismic methods became common. Today calculators and computers are commonly used instead, but abacuses are still in everyday use in some countries. One advantage of the abacus is that you don't need a writing implement and paper (which algorism needs) or an electric power source. Merchants, traders, and clerks use abacuses in some parts of Eastern Europe, Russia, China, and Africa. The abacus is also still commonly used for keeping score in table games that are not electronic. Some people may use an abacus because they have a visual impairment that stops them from using a calculator. In many countries the abacus is still used to teach children the fundamentals of mathematics, such as Japan and China.

steps.text:
An abacus (abaci or abacuses), also called a counting frame, is a hand-operated calculating tool which was used from ancient times, in the ancient Near East, Europe, China, and Russia, until it was largely replaced by handheld electronic calculators during the 1980s, with some ongoing attempts to revive its use.[1,2] An abacus consists of a two-dimensional array of slidable beads (or similar objects). In the earliest designs, the beads could be loose on a flat surface or slide in grooves. Later the beads were made to slide on rods and were built into a frame, allowing faster manipulation.

Each rod typically represents one digit of a multi-digit number laid out using a positional numeral system such as base ten (though some cultures used other numerical bases). Roman and East Asian abacuses use a system resembling bi-quinary coded decimal, with a top deck (containing one or two beads) representing fives and a bottom deck (containing four or five beads) representing ones. Natural numbers are normally used, but some abacuses allow simple fractional components (as in the Roman abacus), and a decimal point can be imagined for fixed-point arithmetic.

Any particular abacus design supports multiple methods of calculation, including addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and square and cube roots. The beads are first arranged to represent a number and then manipulated to perform a mathematical operation with another number; their final position can be read as the result (or used as the starting number for subsequent operations).

In the ancient world, abacuses were a practical calculating tool. The abacus was widely used in Europe as late as the 17th century, but fell out of use with the rise of decimal notation[3] and algorismic methods. Although calculators and computers are commonly used today instead, abacuses remain in everyday use in some countries. The abacus has the advantage of not requiring a writing implement and paper (needed for algorism) or an electric power source. Merchants, traders, and clerks in some parts of Eastern Europe, Russia, China, and Africa use abacuses. The abacus also remains in common use as a scoring system in non-electronic table games, and some people use one because of a visual impairment that prevents them from using a calculator. The abacus is still used to teach the fundamentals of mathematics to children in many countries, such as Japan[4] and China.[5]
